action: Locate the rectus femoris muscle in transverse view. Follow the muscle proximally toward the hip joint and Anterior Inferior Iliac Spine (AIIS).
interpretation: Identify the rectus femoris as an oval-shaped structure. Observe the cross-sectional area becoming progressively smaller as you scan proximally.

action: Continue scanning proximally until the muscle transition is complete.
interpretation: Confirm the transition of the rectus femoris from muscle belly into a tendinous structure.

action: Hold position at the proximal attachment to identify bony landmarks.
interpretation: Visualize the hip joint and the femoral head. Note the rectus femoris is in close proximity, inserting onto the Anterior Inferior Iliac Spine.

action: Highlight the bony landmarks and the tendon insertion.
interpretation: Identify the femoral head and the Anterior Inferior Iliac Spine (AIIS) sloping upward. visualize the hyperechoic tissue of the tendon in this specific area.
Verify that the visualized hyperechoic tissue is indeed the rectus femoris tendon.

action: Slide the transducer from medial to lateral across the insertion point.
interpretation: Visualize the full origin of the tendon at the inferior iliac spine.

action: Inspect the direct tendon for structural integrity.
interpretation: Observe for tendinous changes within the direct tendon. Check for specific signs of avulsion.

action: Scan the area specifically for echogenic artifacts.
interpretation: Search for hyperechoic reflections that would indicate calcifications in this area.

action: Assess the tendon echotexture for pathology.
interpretation: Look for increased hyperechogenicity suggesting tendinopathy. Inspect for anechoic zones within the tendon which would indicate partial tearing.

action: Differentiate between the visible and non-visible tendon components.
interpretation: Note that the direct tendon is visible, but the indirect tendon is not visualized.

action: Evaluate the acoustic limitations of the current probe position.
interpretation: Recognize that the indirect tendon is difficult to see in this position due to obliquity causing full anisotropy.
Note that a different position is required to visualize the indirect tendon.

action: Return the probe to a standard transverse view over the quadriceps. Scan distally, following the rectus femoris down toward knee level.
interpretation: Re-identify the quadriceps and the rectus femoris muscle belly.

action: Focus on the internal architecture of the muscle while scanning.
interpretation: Observe the muscle fibers and the internal tendon (central aponeurosis). Recognize this structure as the aponeurotic expansion of the combined indirect and direct tendons flowing into the muscle belly.
